newsitem.title: ALBANIA: FEATURE - Albania's bunkers -- from Cold War to chicken coop.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Albania's bunkers -- from Cold War to chicken coop.

text.p: Albania's bunkers, one of the most paranoid legacies of its former Stalinist government, are getting a new lease of life -- as chicken coops, mushroom farms, art galleries, cafes and even tiny dank homes.

In a country once so worried about invasion that it placed metal spikes in vineyards to skewer parachutists, Albanians are constantly looking for ways to recycle an estimated 500,000 domed concrete bunkers.
"Even bombs can't hurt us," said Jonuz Kasmi, 47, who lives in his pill-box with walls 30 cm (one foot) thick by a roadside overlooking a river west of Tirana.

"But I can't recommend living in a bunker," he said. Kasmi, his wife and four children, have lived for three-and-a-half years crammed into a space about five metres (16 feet) across and 2.5 metres (eight feet) at the highest point.
He has electricity, water and a gun if needed to defend his family from bandits following the insurrection which swept Albania last month.

Pointing north, south, east, and west -- tiny Albania saw enemies everywhere -- the bunkers drained resources from a desperately poor country that was Europe's most hermetic state for 45 years until communism collapsed in 1990.
"This is probably the only area of the economy where we don't need new investment," said Colonel Qemal Mehmeti of the Defence Ministry.
BUNKERS COST SAME AS A SMALL FLAT

"Too many were built...even in the mountains where there are natural hiding places," he said. "Even the small ones cost 25,000 leks ($2,500 at the time). That was the price of a flat with one or two bedrooms and a kitchen."
Albania began building bunkers as its main fortifications after its ties with the former Soviet Union soured and Tirana pulled out of the Warsaw Pact in 1968.

It turned to China but went it alone in the mid-1970s, angered at Beijing's rapprochement with Washington. Apart from the bunkers and grids of spikes in vineyards, it dug tunnels under cities for air raid shelters.
The feared blitz never came.

Albanians, who had always been told that threats came from abroad, are preparing for the arrival of a multinational Italian-led force to protect aid supplies after the insurrection, triggered by domestic anger at the collapse of savings schemes.
"I keep hay for my cows in my bunker," said Qerim Shala, a 57-year-old farmer west of Tirana.
"I used to have two smaller ones, but an Italian man came along with a crane and pulled them up. It's helped because I can now use the land to grow grapes," he said.
ALBANIAN DEFENCE STILL RELIES ON BUNKERS

Mehmeti reckoned 10 percent of bunkers have been wrecked by people, hit by landslips or choked by weeds. Even so, they remain a key part of Albania's defences -- people can turn them to non-military uses only if they do no structural damage.
"My neighbour keeps chickens in his," said Isuf Hoxha, 71, who has three small bunkers in his 50 metre (yard) garden, including one overgrown by weeds.
"Even during the communist years I never felt protected," he said as a police armoured car rumbled past. "The bunkers disrupted the land, the beaches, our homes. Why? They're useless."

Hoxha, no relation to the late communist dictator Enver Hoxha who built the bunkers, showed off a metal spike that used to be atop a concrete post in his vineyard. "This was for the imperalists!" he laughed, jabbing it skywards.

Near the port of Durres, bunkers along the beach have been converted into seaside cafes. Further south in Qeparo, some Italians have decorated bunkers with bright paintings. Two are painted pink to look like giant breasts.
Many farmers use their bunkers to store farm machinery.
Some people have tried growing mushrooms in the cool soil inside. Others suggest they could be dumped in the sea to make breakwaters to halt erosion or make marinas.

They come in two sizes -- big ones that a handful of people have turned into homes and the smaller, standard size, three metres (10 feet) across that weigh about 25 tonnes. They have a slit on one side for shooting, and an entrance behind.

In the Erzen river between Tirana and the coast, a few dozen shattered bunkers from a bridge-building project lie like giant broken eggshells. So far, there are too few even to break the flow of the river.
Almost no one can afford to blow up bunkers or hire cranes to destroy them. Mehmeti said that under a 1996 law, bunkers cannot normally be moved.
"If a site is to be cleared for a factory, to build flats or a road, for instance, then they can be taken away. But not just to clear farmland," he said.
"They might still be needed. The Balkan region has been unstable. And they are completely defensive," he said.
IN TEST, SOME SHEEP, COWS SURVIVE BUNKER BLITZ

Mehmeti said the design was solid. A 44-year-old career officer, he said he took part in tests under communism, blasting artillery fire at bunkers with sheep or cows inside. "Some of them survived," he said.
Many men in the country of 3.4 million have memories of back-breaking work carrying sacks of material to build bunkers in remote border areas. From 1975, they were pre-fabricated.
Expressing resignation about the presence of the bunkers, one Albanian joke asks: "What did you get from the land privatisation?" The answer: "Two hectares and three bunkers."
Albanian souvenir makers have found a new use for the bunkers -- mini-bunkers in marble are popular with tourists.

And even though many Albanians gripe about the bunkers, some have wistful memories -- bunkers every 50 metres (yards) or so along the beaches of the Adriatic were favoured lovers' hideaways during communism.
